text_en: As referenced in Section 6, the TDRA has introduced performance-level thresholds for indicators defined within this QoS Policy. These indicative thresholds are guides for Licensees on the minimum acceptable level of QoS and QoE delivered to End-users and are therefore primarily for monitoring. However, if the TDRA sees evidence of sustained non-compliance for particular indicator(s) over a period of time, it reserves the right to enforce particular KPI(s) (i.e. mandate Licensees to provide a quality above the defined minimum threshold). The abundant memory resources have no negative impact on slice behaviour, but they affect the overall efficiency of infrastructure resource usage Slice lifecycle KPIs Slice Deployment Time (SDT) SDT is a parameter that describes the interval between the slice deployment request and the moment when the slice is ready for operation. The problem with this parameter is that this interval depends on “slice template (blueprint) complexity”, the performance of the orchestrator, and the allocation of resource time by the virtualised infrastructure. The complexity of a slice is defined by the footprint of the VNFs, the interconnection topology between the different VNFs, and the number of configuration parameters. It is noted that SDT can be critical for some network slices, e.g. in case of on-demand or short-lived ones, but much less critical for long-lived slices. Page 32 Slice lifecycle KPIs Slice Deployment Time Scalability (SDTS) SDTS is a measure of the scalability of slice deployment operations. To evaluate the scalability, it is proposed to send N slice deployment requests for the same slice template and calculate SDTS in the following way: where GSDT is the global time for deployment of N identical slices and SDT is the deployment time for a single slice (as defined above). It is hard to define the N value a priori. If the N value is too large, then there may be a problem with the availability of the requested resources. If it is too small, then the obtained result may not express the scalability of the orchestration well. It is recommended to calculate the SDTS parameter for N = 10. SDTS is expected to be greater than 1. Slice lifecycle KPIs Reconfiguration Execution Time (RET) RET is defined as the interval between a slice reconfiguration request and completion of the slice reconfiguration. It should be noted that RET is not agnostic; that is, it depends on the slice template as well as a number of modifications (number of VNFs, number of links to be reconfigured, number of operations related to VNF reconfiguration). Hence, the expected value of this KPI cannot be defined, but it should be kept as low as possible. RET has a very specific usage in the case of a radio access network (RAN). A RAN can be partly virtualised and may be based on physical network functions (PNFs). In the case of RAN slice reconfiguration, consideration should be given to the change in the area that is served by a slice, by adding and/or removing some RAN nodes. Such operation can still use the RET KPI. However, the value of RET can vary depending on the number of RAN nodes involved in the reconfiguration process. Slice lifecycle KPIs Slice Termination Time (STT) STT is a parameter that describes the interval between a slice termination request and the moment which all slice-allocated resources are released. If this interval is long, the efficiency of infrastructure resource usage will decrease. KPIs for multi-domain slicing In general, there are two options for creating end-to-end slices in multiple domains: • The first is to use a single orchestrator that is able to orchestrate the resources of all domains. • The second is to use a per-domain orchestrator and a higher-level entity in order to co-ordinate the behaviour of domain- level orchestrators and provide the end-to-end operations. Page 33 The first option has the ability to handle domain-specific orchestration issues, but it requires well-defined types of local slices and their descriptors that can be selected for defining the end-to-end slice. From the point of view of KPI calculation, the first option (i.e. based on a single orchestrator) has no impact – they are computed in the same way as in the single-domain case KPIs for multi-domain slicing The second option is much more complicated. Here what is proposed is computation of domain-level KPIs by local operational support systems (OSS) and business support systems (BSS), with this information passing to the end-to-end orchestrator (umbrella network function virtualisation orchestrator (NFVO), which may also perform the role of a local domain NFVO. This orchestrator exposes overall KPIs as well as domain-level KPIs to the end-to-end slice operator and slice tenants. The overall KPIs are computed using the operations on domain-level KPIs of all domains. In some cases, the overall KPIs can be obtained by summing domain-level KPIs, while in other cases, other operations on local KPIs are applicable to determine the overall KPIs. The end-to-end slice set-up time is calculated as the interval between the first domain-level slice set-up request and the last domain-level confirmation of slice deployment. Please note that in contrast to some multi-domain network slicing concepts, a significant role is foreseen for domain-level OSS/BSS.
